label: Jacobi Fields
notes: This chapter, printed pages 283 to 318, studies how nearby geodesics drift apart or refocus. A Jacobi field is the infinitesimal record of that drift, and curvature is the hidden force steering it. We open by previewing the linearized geodesic equation that governs everything that follows.

label: Families of Geodesics
notes: Begin with a smooth one-parameter family of geodesics. Differentiating in the family parameter produces a variation field along the central geodesic. This is the natural source of Jacobi fields, and it ties the abstract equation to a picture of geodesics fanning out from a common origin.

label: The Jacobi Equation
notes: The Jacobi equation is the linearization of the geodesic equation about a fixed geodesic. Differentiating the geodesic condition through the family and commuting covariant derivatives introduces the curvature term, giving a second-order linear ODE along the geodesic that every variation field must satisfy.

label: Existence and Dimension
notes: Because the Jacobi equation is linear and second order, prescribing the field and its covariant derivative at one point determines it uniquely. Along an n-dimensional manifold the solution space has dimension two n, and tangential solutions split off cleanly from the geometrically interesting normal ones.

label: Jacobi Fields and the Exponential Map
notes: The differential of the exponential map is computed by a Jacobi field. A radial geodesic carries a Jacobi field vanishing at the source whose value at the endpoint equals d of the exponential map applied to the initial velocity, turning ODE solutions into chart derivatives.

label: Constant Curvature Solutions
notes: In constant curvature the Jacobi equation has explicit trigonometric solutions. Positive curvature gives sine factors that return to zero, flat space gives linear growth, and negative curvature gives hyperbolic sine factors that grow without bound, exactly mirroring how geodesics focus or spread.

label: Conjugate Points
notes: Two points are conjugate along a geodesic when a nontrivial Jacobi field vanishes at both. Geometrically a whole infinitesimal pencil of geodesics leaving the first point reconverges to the second, signalling that the exponential map is becoming singular there.

label: Conjugacy and the Exponential Map
notes: A point is conjugate exactly when the differential of the exponential map is singular. So conjugate points are critical values of the exponential map, where the radial chart folds and geodesics can stop being locally minimizing beyond that radius.

label: The Second Variation
notes: The second variation of energy at a geodesic yields the index form, a symmetric bilinear form on vector fields built from covariant derivative and curvature terms. Its sign decides whether a geodesic is a genuine local minimum of length among nearby competitors.

label: The Index Form
notes: Integrating by parts rewrites the index form so the Jacobi operator appears explicitly. Jacobi fields are exactly its null directions among fields fixed at the endpoints, which is why conjugate points mark the onset of negative directions and lost minimality.

label: Curvature Controls Focusing
notes: Curvature is the dial for focusing. Positive curvature pulls geodesics back together and forces conjugate points, the sphere being the extreme case with antipodal refocusing. Nonpositive curvature forbids conjugate points entirely, so geodesics spread monotonically and the exponential map stays a local diffeomorphism.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: We close by linking the strands: Jacobi fields measure geodesic spreading, conjugate points mark exponential-map singularities, and the index form converts these into a minimization verdict. This machinery powers comparison theorems and the global results on curvature and topology that follow.
